candidates.stimulus_use: The 'ask who bears the cost' operation turned to the person who pays for stress leakage by avoiding activities such as singing or exercise, and the physiotherapist viewpoint supplied the technique a pelvic health physiotherapist teaches.
candidates.working_title: Squeeze before you cough
candidates.core_insight: Tightening the pelvic floor muscles just before and during a cough or sneeze can reduce stress leakage, and in a small trial older women learned this within a week.
candidates.angle: A timing skill rather than a strength programme: in the original study the benefit did not track pelvic floor strength, so a woman can start using it now while longer supervised training builds strength.
candidates.position: The precontraction (called 'the Knack' in the research) should be taught early to women with stress leakage, alongside supervised pelvic floor muscle training rather than instead of it.
claims_needing_evidence: In a randomised study of 27 women with mild to moderate stress incontinence (mean age 68), contracting the pelvic floor before and during a cough reduced cough-related leakage within 1 week of instruction (primary trial report).
The reduction in leakage was not significantly correlated with a digital measure of pelvic floor strength (same trial report).
NICE recommends supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months as first-line treatment for stress or mixed urinary incontinence in women (NICE guideline).
The technique was tested in selected women with mild to moderate leakage, so the result may not apply to severe leakage (trial inclusion criteria).
evidence_leads: Miller JM, Ashton-Miller JA, DeLancey JO. A pelvic muscle precontraction can reduce cough-related urine loss in selected women with mild SUI. J Am Geriatr Soc 1998;46(7):870-4. PMID 9670874, doi:10.1111/j.1532-5415.1998.tb02721.x (abstract seen on PubMed)

candidates.working_title: A continence service or a pad service?
candidates.core_insight: NICE describes absorbent pads as a way of coping while causes are looked for and treated, so a continence assessment should record a likely cause and a treatment plan as well as a product size.
candidates.angle: Services are named for promoting continence but are often experienced as product supply; the guidance itself sets the standard, which makes this a specific criticism rather than a general complaint.
candidates.position: A pad prescription with no recorded cause and no treatment plan is an incomplete continence assessment.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE states that absorbent products, hand-held urinals and toileting aids should not be considered a treatment for urinary incontinence, and should be used as a coping strategy pending treatment, an adjunct to treatment, or for long-term management only after treatment options have been explored (NICE recommendation text; check exact wording and current numbering).

NHS England's 2018 Excellence in Continence Care guidance describes variation between services and reliance on containment products over assessment and treatment (official guidance; check exact wording).
Family carers of people with dementia described local policies on access to continence products as inconsistent and often inappropriate to their circumstances (qualitative study).

Continence services often report activity as products supplied rather than outcomes such as fewer leaks (would need a service specification, audit or commissioning document; may not be supportable, drop if not).

candidates.angle: Worry about finding a toilet can stop people with urgency going out; a cheap, practical fix is rarely mentioned in clinic.
candidates.position: Continence advice should include how to find and open toilets away from home.

candidates.working_title: Common, often treatable, sometimes persistent
candidates.core_insight: Incontinence becomes more common with age and often improves with treatment, but average improvement in trials is not cure for everyone, so the goal may be fewer leaks, and good care continues when leaking persists.
candidates.angle: Keep the slogan's intent (do not accept leaking as inevitable) while removing its unintended message that persistent incontinence is a personal or clinical failure.
candidates.position: The public message should be that incontinence is common, often improvable, and still deserves good care when it persists.
claims_needing_evidence: The prevalence of urinary incontinence increases with age in women and men (systematic review or International Consultation on Incontinence epidemiology chapter).

In a trial of older women with urge incontinence, behavioural treatment reduced leakage episodes by a mean of about 80% [N to verify]; a mean includes people who improved less (RCT).
Several contributors to incontinence in older people can be reversed, including medicines, constipation, restricted mobility and excess urine output (clinical review).

candidates.working_title: Every catheter needs a leaving date
candidates.core_insight: When someone leaves hospital with a urinary catheter, the letter should say why it went in, when, and who will remove it or try without it, because longer catheter use raises infection risk.
candidates.angle: Each service can reasonably assume the next one owns the removal decision; three written facts break that loop. Catheter passports exist for this purpose.
candidates.position: A catheter without a recorded reason and removal plan at discharge is an incomplete discharge.

Reminder systems and stop orders reduced catheter-associated urinary tract infection rates by about half in hospital studies [N to verify] (meta-analysis).

candidates.core_insight: Loop diuretics such as furosemide produce most of their extra urine in the hours after a dose, so if a water tablet stops you going out, ask the prescriber whether the timing can change rather than skipping it.
candidates.angle: A tablet that controls breathlessness or swelling can be missed on outing days without anyone knowing; a timing conversation protects both the treatment and the person's social life.
candidates.position: Anyone starting a loop diuretic should be asked how it fits their day and told whether the dose time can be moved.

candidates.working_title: The bladder tablet and the teeth
candidates.core_insight: Bladder antimuscarinic tablets had the strongest link with dry mouth of the medicine groups studied in older people, and a dry mouth raises the risk of tooth decay and denture problems, so tell the prescriber and the dentist.

candidates.position: A bladder tablet that has been on repeat for years should be reviewed, and the review should ask about the mouth and teeth as well as leaking.

Reduced saliva increases the risk of dental caries (dental guidance or review).
Sugar-free gum, sips of water or saliva substitutes are advised for dry mouth, and frequent sugary sweets increase decay risk (NHS or dental public health guidance).
In UK prescription data, a minority of people were still on their original antimuscarinic 12 months after starting (prescription database study; industry-funded).

candidates.core_insight: Incontinence is strongly linked with moving into a care home, so when it is driving that decision, ask whether it has been assessed and whether treatment, equipment or night-time help would change things.

Treatable or modifiable contributors to incontinence in older people include constipation, medicines, restricted mobility and excess urine output (clinical review).

candidates.core_insight: In a study of continent adults aged 70 and over, using pads or catheters in hospital was linked with new incontinence at discharge, so helping people to the toilet should be the default.

candidates.working_title: Cranberry: who the evidence covers
candidates.core_insight: The 2023 Cochrane review found cranberry products probably reduce repeat urine infections in women with recurrent infections, but may make little or no difference for older people living in care homes or other institutions.
candidates.angle: Who was studied decides who the result applies to: a finding in women with repeat infections does not transfer to care home residents, and care homes that give cranberry juice to prevent infections are relying on the group where the review found little benefit.
candidates.position: Care homes should not rely on cranberry products to prevent urine infections in residents; for women with recurrent infections living at home, cranberry is a reasonable option to discuss.
claims_needing_evidence: The 2023 Cochrane review included 50 studies with 8,857 participants (systematic review).
In women with recurrent UTIs, cranberry products probably reduced symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs (RR 0.74, moderate certainty) (systematic review).
In older people living in institutions, cranberry products may make little or no difference (3 studies, 1,489 participants, RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.30, moderate certainty) (systematic review).
Absolute effects in plain numbers (N in 100) for each group are available in the review's summary of findings tables [N to verify].

candidates.pause: A popular remedy with a split verdict.
candidates.gain: Knowing whether the evidence applies to the person they care for.
candidates.follow: Shows how to read who a study covers.

candidates.working_title: For men, consider a sheath before a catheter
candidates.core_insight: For men who need urine collected but can empty their bladder, an external sheath avoids a tube in the bladder, was more comfortable in a randomised trial, and was linked with fewer infections or deaths than an indwelling catheter.
candidates.angle: An under-used device that avoids an invasive tube; care that works for men with incontinence who do not have retention, with clear cautions.
candidates.position: For men without retention who need urine collected, a sheath should be considered before an indwelling catheter.
claims_needing_evidence: In a randomised trial of 75 hospitalised men aged 40 and over needing a urine collection device, adverse outcomes (bacteriuria, symptomatic UTI or death) occurred at 70 per 1,000 patient-days with sheaths and 131 per 1,000 with indwelling catheters; the unadjusted difference was not statistically significant and the adjusted analysis was (RCT).
Men rated sheaths as more comfortable and less painful (RCT).
The protective effect was clearest in men without dementia (RCT subgroup analysis).
The CDC guideline suggests considering external catheters for cooperative men without urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction (guideline).
Sheaths need correct sizing and regular skin checks (RCN or product guidance).

candidates.working_title: Once a day is one normal among many
candidates.core_insight: In a Bristol population study, most people did not open their bowels on a regular daily cycle; what signals a problem is hard stools, straining, or a lasting change from your own usual pattern, and a change like that should be checked.
candidates.angle: Relieves the pressure to go every day that can drive unnecessary laxative use, while making clear which changes need a doctor.
candidates.position: A change from your own usual pattern tells you more than a daily count.
claims_needing_evidence: In a random sample of about 1,900 adults in East Bristol, once-daily bowel opening was the most common pattern but a minority practice, and most people had irregular bowels (population study).
Bowel frequency between about three times a day and three times a week is common in healthy people [N to verify] (population study; NHS information).
Constipation is defined by infrequent stools together with hard stools or straining (NHS information or Rome criteria).
A persistent change in bowel habit, blood in the stool or unexplained weight loss in older adults should be assessed promptly (NICE NG12).

candidates.working_title: The bowel leakage people rarely mention
candidates.core_insight: Accidental bowel leakage becomes more common with age, often has treatable causes, and most people who have it never tell a doctor.
candidates.angle: Gives the reader words to raise it, and what a GP or nurse can check.
candidates.position: Bowel leakage is worth raising with a GP or practice nurse, because many of its causes can be treated.
claims_needing_evidence: In a US survey of adults attending primary care or gastroenterology, faecal incontinence became more common with age, and only about a third of people with it had ever discussed it with a doctor (survey study).
Common causes include loose stools, constipation with overflow, weak or damaged anal sphincter muscles, neurological conditions and medicines (NICE CG49).
Treatments include adjusting diet and fibre, treating constipation or diarrhoea, medicines such as loperamide where appropriate, pelvic floor and sphincter exercises and bowel retraining (NICE CG49).

candidates.gain: The words to start the conversation and what to expect.
candidates.follow: Treats embarrassing problems directly and respectfully.

candidates.working_title: Moisture damage or pressure damage?
candidates.core_insight: Skin damage from contact with urine or stool (incontinence-associated dermatitis) looks different from a pressure ulcer and needs different care: gentle pH-balanced cleansing, a barrier product and prompt changes.
candidates.angle: Misclassification leads to the wrong care and the wrong incident report; a structured tool helps staff tell the two apart.
candidates.position: Services caring for people with incontinence should use a structured way to tell moisture damage from pressure damage.
claims_needing_evidence: Incontinence-associated dermatitis is skin inflammation caused by prolonged contact with urine or stool (expert consensus).

It tends to be diffuse and superficial, in perineal, genital and buttock areas where moisture is present, whereas pressure ulcers usually occur over bony prominences (expert consensus; pressure ulcer guideline).
Guidance recommends cleansing with a pH-balanced product and applying a skin protectant, rather than soap and water (expert consensus).
The Ghent Global IAD Categorisation Tool is a published tool for categorising incontinence-associated dermatitis (validation study; unsure).

candidates.follow: Useful teaching for nurses and care workers as well as doctors.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E112 covers pressure ulcers after hip fracture; this post teaches the distinction from moisture damage.

candidates.working_title: One well-fitted pad works better than two
candidates.core_insight: Layering two pads, or a pad over a bed protector, often makes leaks and sore skin more likely, because the waterproof backing of the inner layer stops urine reaching the outer one and traps heat and moisture.
candidates.angle: A practice that comes from good intentions (fewer changes, fewer wet beds) and has the opposite effect; the fix is the right size and absorbency, fitted properly.
candidates.position: Double padding should be replaced by one correctly sized pad of the right absorbency, fitted properly.
claims_needing_evidence: Most continence pads have a waterproof backing, so a second pad worn over the first does not absorb urine held back by the first (product design; manufacturer or NHS continence service guidance).
Continence service and expert guidance advise against layering pads or pads and bed protectors (NHS continence service guidance or IAD expert consensus; unsure which).
Occlusion and prolonged moisture raise the risk of incontinence-associated dermatitis (expert consensus).
evidence_leads: Beeckman D et al. Global IAD Expert Panel 2015 (unsure whether layering of pads is addressed)

candidates.pause: Care workers and families who double pad will recognise the habit.
candidates.gain: A simple change that can reduce leaks and skin damage.
candidates.follow: Respects care workers by explaining why, not only what.

candidates.working_title: Name the reason for the catheter
candidates.core_insight: An indwelling urinary catheter should have a reason you can name, such as retention or hourly output monitoring in critical illness, and the CDC guideline lists using one in place of nursing care for incontinence as inappropriate.
candidates.angle: A short list of valid reasons; stop orders and reminders roughly halve infection rates; and catheters restrict movement, which one commentary described as a 'one-point restraint'.
candidates.position: No catheter should be inserted or kept without a documented reason, and nurses should be able to remove one that no longer has a reason.
claims_needing_evidence: The CDC guideline lists appropriate indications (acute retention or obstruction, accurate output measurement in critically ill patients, selected surgery, healing of open sacral or perineal wounds in incontinent patients, prolonged immobilisation, comfort at the end of life) and inappropriate uses, including as a substitute for nursing care of incontinence (guideline).

The HOUDINI nurse-led removal protocol lists indications for continuing a catheter (protocol publication; unsure).

candidates.working_title: Nocturia: measure the volumes, not only the trips
candidates.core_insight: Getting up at night to pass urine has two common patterns, making too much urine at night or a bladder that holds less, and a bladder diary with measured volumes tells them apart, which changes treatment.
candidates.angle: The common shortcut (a bladder tablet, or blaming the prostate) misses nocturnal polyuria from heart failure, ankle swelling, evening drinks, diuretic timing or sleep apnoea; desmopressin carries a sodium risk in older people.
candidates.position: Nocturia in an older person should be assessed with a frequency-volume chart before any drug is started.
claims_needing_evidence: The International Continence Society defined nocturnal polyuria in older adults as night-time urine above a third of the 24-hour volume, a threshold some studies consider too low [N to verify] (ICS terminology; reference population study).

Causes of nocturnal polyuria include heart failure, peripheral oedema, evening fluid, caffeine or alcohol, diuretic timing, obstructive sleep apnoea and poorly controlled diabetes (ICS report or guideline).
NICE recommends a frequency-volume chart in assessing men with lower urinary tract symptoms (NICE CG97).
Desmopressin carries a risk of hyponatraemia that is higher in older people, and NICE advises checking sodium after starting it (NICE CG97 or MHRA; check wording).

candidates.working_title: Drinking less to leak less
candidates.core_insight: Cutting right down on drinks to avoid leaks is a common coping strategy that can bring other problems; NICE advises adjusting fluid intake only when it is too high or too low, and trying less caffeine for urgency.
candidates.angle: A familiar coping strategy with neglected consequences (constipation, dizziness, concentrated urine), and practical alternatives.
candidates.position: Older people with leaks or urgency should be advised on what and when to drink, rather than simply to drink less.
claims_needing_evidence: Some community-dwelling older adults with incontinence restrict fluids as a coping strategy (survey study; small).
NICE recommends a trial of caffeine reduction for women with overactive bladder and advises modifying high or low fluid intake (NICE NG123).
Low fluid intake is associated with constipation in older people (review or guideline; unsure of strength).
Concentrated urine may irritate the bladder and worsen urgency (weak evidence; drop if not supported).

candidates.working_title: Pelvic floor classes worked as well as one-to-one
candidates.core_insight: In a trial of 362 women aged 60 and over with stress or mixed leakage, 12 weeks of group pelvic floor classes reduced leaks as much as one-to-one physiotherapy at one year, which could let more women get a first-line treatment.
candidates.angle: Care that works and service design: a way to widen access; every woman had one individual session first to learn the contraction, and improvement on average came by about week 4.
candidates.position: Services with long waits for pelvic health physiotherapy should offer group classes for older women, after an individual session to check technique.
claims_needing_evidence: In the GROUP trial (362 community-dwelling women aged 60 and over, mean age 68), the median reduction in leakage episodes at 1 year was 74% with group training and 70% with individual training, meeting the non-inferiority margin (RCT).
All women had one individual session to learn to contract the pelvic floor before the 12-week programme (RCT methods).
In a pooled analysis of the trial, a clinically important reduction in leakage was reached by a median of about 4 weeks [N to verify] (secondary analysis).
NICE recommends supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months as first-line treatment for stress or mixed incontinence (NICE NG123).

candidates.working_title: Dribbling can mean a full bladder

candidates.working_title: Looking after your own pessary
candidates.core_insight: In a UK trial, women taught to remove and replace their own vaginal pessary for prolapse had similar quality of life to women who attended clinic for it, reported fewer complications, and the approach was cost-effective.
candidates.angle: Care that works that respects agency and saves clinic trips; the trial excluded women with limited dexterity or cognitive impairment, so clinic care remains for those who need it.
candidates.position: Women using a pessary who are able to manage it should be offered teaching to look after it themselves.
claims_needing_evidence: In the TOPSY trial (340 women, UK centres), self-management and clinic-based care showed no difference in prolapse-specific quality of life at 18 months (RCT).
More pessary complications were reported in the clinic-based group at 18 months (RCT).
Self-management was cost-effective at the usual UK threshold (RCT economic evaluation).

candidates.working_title: New leaking after a dementia medicine
candidates.core_insight: Cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil can cause or worsen urinary incontinence, and in a large cohort people started on them were more likely to be prescribed a bladder antimuscarinic, a drug with the opposite action.
candidates.angle: A prescribing cascade: the new leak is read as a new condition, a second drug with opposing pharmacology is added, and anticholinergic load rises.
candidates.position: New or worse incontinence after starting a cholinesterase inhibitor should lead to a review of that drug before a bladder drug is added.

candidates.working_title: Continence care after a dementia diagnosis
candidates.core_insight: People with dementia are often moved straight to pads, but causes such as constipation, medicines, difficulty finding the toilet and not being prompted can still be addressed, and prompted toileting helped some care home residents who could follow a simple instruction.
candidates.angle: An evidence gap (several key continence trials excluded people with dementia) can turn into a practice default; families often get help late and inconsistently.
candidates.position: People with dementia deserve the same search for the causes of incontinence as anyone else.
claims_needing_evidence: Several key trials of behavioural continence treatment in older people excluded people with dementia (trial methods, for example Burgio 1998).
Family carers of people with dementia often sought professional help with incontinence late, and reported unhelpful responses and inconsistent product policies (qualitative study).
Prompted voiding helped a proportion of nursing home residents who passed a simple screen of being able to state their name or point to a named object (cohort study).
Treatable contributors such as constipation, medicines and environmental barriers apply to people with dementia (clinical review).
